listening.title: Riverton Bus-Fare Pilot Evaluation
listening.focus: Causal limits and sampling bias in transport policy evidence
listening.script:
Maya: Hi Jonah, have you finished reading the evaluation of the Riverton bus-fare pilot for our transport policy seminar?
Jonah: Mostly. The city cut all bus fares by 50% from April to June last year to test whether cheaper fares would encourage regular commuters to switch from cars, right?
Maya: Yes, that was the official aim in the council brief — to see if lower costs would shift daily commuting patterns, not just leisure trips.
Jonah: I wrote down it ran from March to May, actually sorry, April to June — I misread the dates. Three months total. The report says weekday ridership rose 18% compared to January to March.
Maya: That's the headline increase, but we have to be careful about causality. In May, petrol prices rose 22% citywide, so driving became much more expensive during the same period.
Jonah: So we can't tell how much of the rise was due to the fare cut versus people avoiding high fuel costs.
Maya: Exactly. And there was no control group — no similar city or unaffected bus route to compare against. Without that, any causal claim is weak.
Jonah: What about the passenger survey? It said 78% of respondents would continue using the bus if fares stayed low.
Maya: But that survey was voluntary, conducted at the central terminal on weekdays. The authors note respondents were self-selected — mainly frequent riders who benefited most.
Jonah: So it overrepresents enthusiastic users and underrepresents occasional riders or those who didn't change behaviour.
Maya: Right, that's a classic selection bias. The report acknowledges the sample isn't representative of all residents.
Jonah: So for our presentation, we shouldn't say the pilot proved cheaper fares work.
Maya: No, we should conclude the evidence is suggestive but inconclusive. We can recommend a longer, controlled trial with random sampling across routes and neighbourhoods to get a clearer picture.
Jonah: That makes sense. We'll emphasize the limits and propose a better design rather than claiming success.

questions.title: Purpose of Pilot
questions.prompt: What was the council's stated aim for the fare reduction?
options: Encourage daily commuters to switch from cars
Increase leisure travel on weekends
Test electric buses on busy routes
Reduce traffic congestion downtown only
questions.explanation: The brief aimed to shift daily commuting from cars, not leisure trips. Option B reverses the stated scope.

questions.title: Pilot Dates
questions.prompt: What correction does Jonah make about the pilot period?
options: It lasted two months, not three
It ran April to June, not March to May
It started in January, not April
It ended in July, not June
questions.explanation: Jonah first says March to May then corrects to April to June. Option A misstates the correction as duration.

questions.title: Causal Limitation
questions.prompt: Why can't the ridership rise be attributed solely to cheaper fares?
options: Bus drivers went on strike in May
Ticket machines failed to record data
Petrol prices increased sharply during pilot
Weather was unusually cold that quarter
questions.explanation: Petrol prices rose 22% at the same time, offering a competing explanation. Option A invents a strike not mentioned.

questions.title: Survey Weakness
questions.prompt: What problem do they identify with the passenger survey?
options: It was conducted only online after pilot
It excluded all weekday travellers
It asked only about leisure trips
It overrepresented enthusiastic frequent riders
questions.explanation: The voluntary terminal survey was self-selected toward frequent beneficiaries. Option A incorrectly claims it was online.

questions.title: Presentation Conclusion
questions.prompt: What will they argue in their presentation?
options: Pilot proved fare cuts always increase ridership
Results are inconclusive and need controlled follow-up
Survey data should be ignored completely
Fuel prices had no effect on travel
questions.explanation: They plan to call evidence suggestive but inconclusive and recommend a controlled trial. Option A overclaims proof.

reading.title: Volunteer Heat Maps and Education Rankings
reading.focus: Selection bias and measurement uncertainty in policy data
reading.passage:
Cities increasingly rely on low-cost data to guide climate policy. One popular method is the volunteer heat survey, where residents use handheld sensors to record street-level temperatures during a heatwave. These campaigns generate detailed maps and raise public awareness, but they also introduce systematic errors that are often overlooked in media reports. Policymakers may be tempted to treat these maps as complete, but without understanding who participated, they risk misallocating cooling resources to already comfortable neighbourhoods.

The 2022 Riverton Heat Watch illustrates the problem. Organisers recruited 140 volunteers through neighbourhood associations and social media. Participation was voluntary, and the resulting sample was geographically skewed: 68% of readings came from the greener, wealthier northern districts, where tree cover is high and housing is less dense. Only 12% came from the industrial south, where asphalt and warehouses trap heat. Because volunteers chose where and when to measure, often near their homes on pleasant streets, the dataset overrepresented cooler areas. The published citywide average of 31.4°C therefore understated true exposure; an independent network of calibrated fixed air-temperature sensors, recording at the same afternoon hour with even coverage across districts, recorded a citywide average of 33.6°C and an average of 35.9°C in the industrial south. The example does not prove volunteers are unmotivated; it shows how self-selection shapes coverage.

The author argues that such surveys should not be dismissed, but their scope must be qualified. They are valuable for identifying relative hotspots within sampled areas and for community engagement, yet they cannot support precise citywide estimates or causal claims about the effectiveness of cooling interventions without statistical adjustment for sampling bias. The limitation is not the volunteers' effort but the lack of random, representative coverage. Weighting results by district population or supplementing with satellite data can reduce bias, but such corrections are rarely applied in initial press releases.

A similar issue of uncertainty appears in cross-country education indicators. International reports often rank countries by secondary-school completion rates, implying direct comparability. However, national definitions of "completion" differ — some count part-time vocational programmes, others do not — and data collection varies from census to sample surveys. A country reporting 89% completion may appear superior to one reporting 82%, but the gap may reflect measurement differences rather than real achievement. The passage notes that year-to-year changes within a single country, using a consistent method, are more reliable than cross-country league tables at a single point in time.

Together, these cases suggest a general principle: data collected for different purposes or through non-random methods require careful interpretation. Recognising who is missing, how definitions vary, and what comparisons are warranted prevents overclaiming and leads to more honest policy. Transparency about methods and limits, rather than precise rankings, builds greater trust in the evidence.

questions.title: Function of Volunteer Surveys
questions.prompt: According to the passage, what do volunteer heat surveys provide?
options: Precise citywide temperature averages for policy
Detailed maps and public engagement despite errors
Satellite data to replace street sensors
Proof that tree cover has no effect
questions.explanation: The passage says they generate detailed maps and raise awareness despite systematic errors. Option A claims precision the author denies.

questions.title: Riverton Sampling Bias
questions.prompt: Why did Riverton's average understate heat exposure?
options: Most readings came from cooler northern districts
Volunteers measured only at night
Sensors were faulty in industrial areas
Satellite data was not included
questions.explanation: 68% of readings came from greener northern districts, overrepresenting cooler areas. Option B invents a night-only method.

questions.title: Claim Versus Example
questions.prompt: What does the author claim about volunteer surveys?
options: Volunteers lacked motivation to measure accurately
Surveys are useless for any policy purpose
They are useful for hotspots but not precise citywide estimates
Satellite data proves volunteers measured correctly
questions.explanation: The author says they are valuable for hotspots and engagement but cannot support precise citywide estimates without adjustment. Option A is explicitly rejected by the example.

questions.title: Education Comparison Inference
questions.prompt: What can be inferred about comparing 89% and 82% completion rates?
options: The 7% gap definitely shows better achievement
Both countries used identical census methods
Vocational programmes are always excluded
The gap may reflect measurement differences, not achievement
questions.explanation: The passage notes differing definitions and methods may explain the gap. Option A overstates certainty the author warns against.

questions.title: Overall Principle
questions.prompt: What general principle do both cases illustrate?
options: Non-random data need careful interpretation to avoid overclaiming
Volunteer data should never guide policy decisions
International rankings are always more reliable than local trends
Statistical adjustment eliminates all uncertainty
questions.explanation: Both cases show non-random or inconsistently defined data require qualified interpretation. Option B is too absolute; the author says not to dismiss surveys.
